questions.question: Q1. According to Timoshenko's formula, what thickness ratio (m = h1/h2) maximizes curvature for layers with equal Young's Modulus (n = E1/E2 = 1)?

answers.d: Curvature is independent of thickness ratio.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Very thin active layers produce negligible bending force.
explanations.b: Correct — When elastic moduli are equal (n=1), the maximum curvature is obtained exactly at a thickness ratio of m = h1/h2 = 1.0.
explanations.c: Incorrect — At m=2, the passive layer becomes too thin to optimally resist and transfer strain, reducing curvature.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Curvature depends heavily on the thickness ratio.

questions.question: Q2. In Sub-Calc C, if you program a bilayer with a top print angle of 45° and a bottom print angle of -45°, what deformation mode is primarily observed upon heating?

answers.a: Pure flat bending along the longitudinal axis.
answers.b: Torsional twisting (torsion) along the beam axis.
answers.c: Uniform isotropic expansion without out-of-plane motion.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Orthogonal symmetric angle combinations like 0°/90° lead to flat bending.
explanations.b: Correct — Antisymmetric angle combinations like 45°/-45° align the principal expansion axes diagonally, producing pure twisting.
explanations.c: Incorrect — The mismatch in shear strains leads to out-of-plane twisting.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The deformation is a stable torsional twist, not random buckling.

questions.question: Q3. If the active layer thickness of a moisture-driven actuator is doubled (from 0.5 mm to 1.0 mm), how does the time to reach 90% swelling equilibrium (t90) change?

answers.d: It remains unchanged because the diffusion coefficient is constant.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Diffusion time does not scale linearly with thickness.
explanations.b: Correct — Since t90 ∝ L², doubling the thickness (2L) increases the diffusion time by a factor of 2² = 4.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Thicker layers take longer to reach equilibrium, not less time.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Diffusion time depends strongly on layer thickness.

questions.question: Q4. Under what condition does the small-deflection Timoshenko linear assumption fail, requiring the use of a Nonlinear Elastica solver?

answers.a: When the temperature change (ΔT) is negative.
answers.b: When the product of curvature and length (κL) exceeds 0.3.
answers.c: When the Young's modulus ratio (n) is less than 1.0.
answers.d: When the width of the beam is greater than the length.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Negative ΔT simply reverses the bending direction, which can still be linear.
explanations.b: Correct — The linear beam assumption requires small deflections; once κL > 0.3, geometric nonlinearities become significant and require Nonlinear Elastica solvers.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Modulus ratio has no bearing on the validity of small-deflection geometric assumptions.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Beam width relates to plate behavior, not the geometric deflection limit.

questions.question: Q5. How does the blocking force (Fblock) scale with the total thickness (h) of a bilayer actuator cantilever?

answers.c: Proportional to the square of thickness (Fblock ∝ h²).
answers.d: Proportional to the cube of thickness (Fblock ∝ h³).

explanations.a: Incorrect — Thicker beams are stiffer and generate much higher forces.
explanations.b: Incorrect — The scaling is much stronger than linear.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Scaling is cubic, not quadratic.
explanations.d: Correct — The bending stiffness of a cantilever scales with the cube of its thickness (h³), directly scaling the blocking force by h³.

questions.question: Q6. Why does a 0°/90° print raster combination produce maximum out-of-plane bending rather than twisting?

answers.a: Because the shear coupling term (η_xy) for both layers is zero, preventing twist.
answers.b: Because the materials used have no shear modulus.
answers.c: Because the temperature change cancels out the shear strains.
answers.d: Because the print lines are oriented along the diagonals.

explanations.a: Correct — At 0° and 90°, the principal expansion axes align perfectly with the longitudinal and transverse axes, making shear strain coupling zero and preventing twisting.
explanations.b: Incorrect — All solid materials have a shear modulus.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Temperature changes drive the strain; they do not cancel shear strains unless aligned properly.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The lines are parallel/perpendicular to the boundaries, not diagonal.

questions.question: Q7. An actuator has a blocking force of 20 mN and a free deflection of 4 mm. What is its work output under linear assumptions?

explanations.a: Incorrect — Work is 0.5 × Fblock × delta_free, not the simple product.

questions.question: Q8. In hygroscopic swelling of cellulose composites, what role does the Swelling Anisotropy Ratio (As) play in determining curvature?

answers.a: A higher As (with fibers transverse to length) yields greater out-of-plane curvature because the transverse strain mismatch is larger.
answers.b: A higher As reduces bending because the fibers restrict all motion.
answers.c: As only changes the temperature at which swelling starts.
answers.d: It has no effect; only total moisture uptake matters.

explanations.a: Correct — A high swelling anisotropy means that when fibers are oriented at 90° (transverse), they expand much more along the beam length than the passive layer, creating a larger strain mismatch and greater bending.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Anisotropy enables, rather than restricts, curvature programming by orienting the high-expansion direction.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Swelling is driven by moisture, not temperature, and As is a strain ratio.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Isotropic swelling creates spherical curvature, while anisotropic swelling allows directional bending.

questions.question: Q9. How does the diffusion coefficient (D) of the active material affect the response speed of a bilayer actuator?

answers.a: A larger D decreases the diffusion speed, making actuation slower.
answers.b: A larger D increases the diffusion speed, making actuation faster.
answers.c: D only affects the maximum deflection, not the speed.
answers.d: D is always zero in solid actuators.

explanations.a: Incorrect — A larger diffusion coefficient speeds up the transport, making it faster.
explanations.b: Correct — The characteristic diffusion time tdiff ∝ L² / D, so a larger D results in a smaller tdiff (faster response).
explanations.c: Incorrect — D governs kinetic rate, not thermodynamic swelling limit.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Polymeric and hydrogel solid materials have non-zero diffusion coefficients for solvents.

questions.question: Q10. What is the main design trade-off when reducing active layer thickness (L) to speed up a moisture-driven actuator?

answers.a: It increases the cost of materials significantly.
answers.b: Thinner active layers actuate faster but generate less blocking force and lower work output.
answers.c: Thinner layers will completely prevent any bending from occurring.
answers.d: Thinner layers decrease the diffusion coefficient.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Thinner layers actually use less material, reducing cost.
explanations.b: Correct — While thinning the layer reduces diffusion time (speeding up response), it also decreases the bending stiffness and the generated force (Fblock ∝ h³), reducing total work output.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Bending still occurs, but the structural force generated is weaker.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The diffusion coefficient is a material property, independent of thickness.
